et: Middle English {it}grosse, groce{/it} "large, thick, coarse, not in detail, plain," borrowed from Anglo-French {it}gros, grosse{/it} "large, great, fat, pregnant, important, (of flour, salt) coarse" (also continental Old French), going back to Latin {it}grossus{/it} "thick," "unripe," of uncertain origin

The Latin adjective {it}grossus{/it} occurs in some manuscripts of {it}De re rustica{/it} by the Roman agricultural writer Columella (1st century {sc}a.d.{/sc}), taking the place of, in other witnesses, {it}crassus{/it} "thick" and {it}crūdus{/it} "unripe." It is difficult to separate this word etymologically from the noun {it}grossus{/it} (or {it}grossa{/it}), used by agricultural writers and Pliny to refer to an unripe or abortive fig. As an adjective in a variety of senses, {it}grossus{/it} has outcomes in nearly all the Romance languages and dialects.
